holidays.name: National Hug a Plumber Day
holidays.description: A day to thank the people who rescue us from clogged drains, burst pipes and mystery gurgles. Give your plumber a hug, or at least a warm thank-you and a cold drink.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance and its origin is unclear. It has become a popular way to honor the skilled tradespeople behind modern indoor plumbing.
holidays.funFact: Plumbing is one of the oldest skilled trades. Ancient civilizations such as the Indus Valley and Rome built sophisticated water and drainage systems, and the word 'plumber' comes from the Latin 'plumbum', meaning lead.

holidays.name: National Zucchini Bread Day
holidays.description: A salute to the moist, lightly spiced quick bread that sneaks a vegetable into dessert. It is also the perfect excuse to use up the zucchini that gardeners can't stop producing.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. Zucchini bread grew popular in North American home kitchens as a clever way to use a garden glut.
holidays.funFact: A single zucchini plant can produce so much fruit that gardeners have been known to leave bags of it on neighbors' porches. Zucchini is technically a fruit, since it grows from the plant's flower and holds seeds.

holidays.name: DNA Day
holidays.description: A celebration of the double helix and the science of genetics. Schools, labs and science fans mark it with lessons, activities and a nod to the molecule that makes you, you.
holidays.origin: It commemorates April 25, 1953, when James Watson, Francis Crick and colleagues published papers describing the double-helix structure of DNA. It also marks the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003.
holidays.funFact: If you uncoiled the DNA in just one human cell, it would stretch about two meters, yet it fits inside a nucleus far smaller than a speck of dust.
